subject: cost of more general user defined functions

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: cost of more general user defined functions
parts:
Hi!

Nowadays I tend to write pretty general user defined functions for my models and I wonder what the numeric cost is if I add more arguments to the function which I only call with data arguments. An example:

# simple function
matrix foo(real a, real b) {
  # do complex stuff here
  return(result);
}

Now suppose I call foo in my model block with a and b being parameters in the model. The autodiff will calculate gradients wrt to a and b. However, what if I extend that function to

# expanded function
matrix foo2(real a, real b, real c) {
  # do more general complex stuff here
  return(result);
}


But I call again in my model block the function foo2 with a and b being parameters while variable c was declared in the transformed data block (for example). The question is: Does this increase the cost for autodiff during sampling?

I am asking as it can be convenient to make functions more complex than possilby needed during the inference step, i.e. during simulation it may be more convenient to have a more general function.

Many thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] cost of more general user defined functions
parts:
It would help to know what you're doing, because it
depends on what the "complex stuff" is.

The point is that every expression that gets evaluated
and assigned to a temporary or used in an operation with
a parameter adds to the autodiff cost.

To be more concrete, with

matrix foo(real y, real mu) {
return normal_log(y, mu, 1);
}

and

matrix foo(real y, real mu, real sigma) {
return normal_log(y, mu, sigma);
}

calling foo(y, mu) vs. foo(y, mu, 1) will have the same cost.
So passing data in doesn't intrinsically have any cost (at least not
one you're going to be able to measure).

- Bob

Thanks Bob, this answers my question, i.e. specifically I intend to make the initial PK concentration of each patient in my population a parameter. That is, during inference this will be set to 0 for time t=0 for all patients, but for simulation purposes I find it more convenient to have a function which can start simulating a patient from different initials.

Best,
Sebastian
